record.paper_title: Some of my favorite open problems
record.original_question: Consider smooth maps u:R^2→R^2≈C solving Δu=u(1-|u|^2) on R^2 and satisfying |u(x)|→1 as |x|→∞. For each integer q, let V_q(r,θ)=e^{iqθ}g_q(r), where g_q is the unique radial profile with g_q(0)=0 and g_q(r)→1 as r→∞, and let deg(u,∞) be the degree at infinity. Must every such solution u be of the form αV_q(x-x_0) for some q=deg(u,∞), some α∈C with |α|=1, and some translation x_0∈R^2?

evidence.quote: A long-standing open problem is whether the functions Vq, q ∈ Z, are the only solutions of (2.4)-(2.5); more precisely: Open Problem 2.4 ... Let u be any solution of (2.4)-(2.5). Does u coincide with Vq modulo rotation and translation, where q = deg(u,∞)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $u:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2\cong\mathbb{C}$ be a smooth solution of the Ginzburg–Landau equation
$$\Delta u = u(1-|u|^2)\quad\text{on }\mathbb{R}^2,$$
satisfying the condition at infinity $|u(x)|\to 1$ as $|x|\to\infty$. Under these hypotheses one can define the degree at infinity $\deg(u,\infty)\in\mathbb{Z}$, namely the winding number of $u/|u|$ along a sufficiently large circle.

For each integer $q$, it is known that there exists a unique radial profile $g_q:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ with $g_q(0)=0$ and $g_q(r)\to 1$ as $r\to\infty$ such that the map
$$V_q(r,\theta) := e^{iq\theta} g_q(r)$$
solves the equation above (in polar coordinates $(r,\theta)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$) and has degree $q$ at infinity.

Question: must every such solution $u$ be of the form
$$u(x) = \alpha\, V_q(x-x_0)$$
for some $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\alpha|=1$, some $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^2$, and $q=\deg(u,\infty)$?
artifact.status_search_result: The classification of entire solutions of the planar Ginzburg–Landau equation with $|u|\to 1$ at infinity as the equivariant vortices $V_q$ (modulo translation and constant phase) is a long-standing open problem, raised in the Bethuel–Brezis–Hélein book and reiterated in subsequent surveys. Recent progress (Ignat, Nguyen, Slastikov, Zarnescu and collaborators) has established uniqueness/minimality of the degree-one vortex in balls in dimensions $N\ge 7$ and various symmetry/minimality results, but the full classification on $\mathbb{R}^2$ remains unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Minimality of the vortex solution for Ginzburg-Landau systems (Ignat, MFO report 2024)
status_evidence.snippet: The question of uniqueness in dimension N = 2 for the disk was raised in the seminal book of Bethuel, Brezis and Hélein (Problem 10, page 139) ... remains open in low dimensions.
status_evidence.claim: The uniqueness/classification of vortex solutions in two dimensions is identified as an open problem.

status_evidence.title: Uniqueness of degree-one Ginzburg-Landau vortex in the unit ball in dimensions N ≥ 7
status_evidence.snippet: For N ≥ 7 the equivariant vortex is the unique minimizer; the lower-dimensional cases including N=2 remain open.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress exists in higher dimensions, but the planar entire-solution classification is not settled.
